Implementation of power projects 
*101.     SHRIMATI AMBIKA SONI:† 
 DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: 
Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether of the 44 power projects under implementation currently, 39 
projects are slated to come up by the first year of the Eleventh Five Year Plan 
period; 
(b) if so, whether 5 projects are reported to be facing constraints in timely 
commissioning; 
(c) the total projects that are being completed within the stipulated period 
of time and how many will be there which will not be completed; 
(d) whether any guidelines had been issued by the Ministry of Statistics 
and Programme Implementation to the Ministry of Power in this regard; and 
(e) if so, what steps are being taken by the Ministry of Power to 
implement suggestions made by the Ministry of Statistics and Programme 
Implementation? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI P.M. SAYEED): (a) to (e) A 
Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) to (e) No, Sir. In the month of May, 2005, out of the 313 projects 
costing Rs. 100 crore and above being monitored by Ministry of Statistics

RAJYA SABHA [30 November, 2005] 
and Programme Implementation (MOS&PI), 44 projects pertained to power 
sector. Out of this, 31 projects were expected to be completed in 10th Plan, 
12 projects are slated to come in th e 11th Plan and the remaining 1 is 
currently under hold. Out of the 31 projects to be completed in 10th Plan, 8 
have since commissioned. 
However, as per the monitoring being done in the Ministry of Power, at 
present 71 Central Sector power projects with a total cost of Rs. 1,31,670 
crore are under execution.  Out of these projects, 31 pertain to generation 
segment and remaining 40 to transmission sector. Out of these projects, 31 
are to be completed within X Plan and remaining 40 are likely to be 
commissioned in the XI Plan. 
Out of the 71 projects under execution under the Central Sector, 6 projects 
have reported time overrun. Out of this, 4 are expected to be commissioned 
within X Plan and remaining 2 would be completed in the XI Plan. 
No guidelines have been issued to the Ministry of Power in this regard by 
the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation. However, 
following measures have been adopted for timely commissioning of the 
power generation projects:— 
> The monitoring mechanism has been strengthened. 
> The CEA has a nodal officer for each project, both at the conception 
stage as well as during execution. 
> Regular reivew meetings are being organized in the Ministry of Power 
with a view to identifying problems and facilitating their resolution. 
The average execution time for power projects has declined in the country.

THE MINISTER OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT (SHRI RAGHUVANSH 
PRASAD SINGH): (a) to (e) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) SGSY is not Sampoorna Gramin Swarozgar Yojana but it is 
Swarnjayanti Gram Swarozgar Yojana. It  is a self-employment scheme aims 
at establishing a large number of micro enterprises in rural areas based on the 
ability of the poor and potential of each area. The objective of the scheme is 
to bring the assisted poor families (S warozgaris) above the poverty line by 
organizing them into Self Help Groups (SHGs) and providing them income 
generating assets through a mix of bank credit and government subsidy. The 
scheme is financed on 75:25 cost sharing basis between the Centre and the 
States. Funds under the scheme are re leased directly to District Rural 
Development Agencies (DRDAs). 
Government have not failed to spend funds allocated under SGSY Central 
allocation of funds during current financial year (2005-06) for Swarnjayanti 
Gram Swarozgar Yojana (SGSY) is Rs. 1000.00 crore which is the same as 
allocated during 2004-05. Release of funds under Swaranjayanti Gram

(c) to (e) Funds allocated under the scheme have been almost fully utilized 
during the last three years. To ensure proper and effective utilization of funds 
under SGSY, scheme is monitored from the Central level down to the grass 
root level. At the Central level, the Central Level Co-ordination Committee 
(CLCC) monitors and reviews the implementation of the scheme and lays 
down policy guidelines for all aspects relating to the credit linkages for the 
SGSY. At the State level, a State Le vel of SGSY Committee monitors the 
programme. In addition, the progress under SGSY is monitored periodically 
through reports and returns submitted by the DRDAs/States. Implementation 
of the Programme is monitored and rviewed through the Annual Project 
Directors Workshop and periodic Perf ormance Review Committee meetings 
with the State Secretarie s. At the Block/DRDA level monitoring is done 
through field visits and physical verification of assets. In addition, the 
programme is also monitored through other monitoring machanism of the 
Ministry like vigilance and Monitori ng Committee, Area Officers Scheme, 
District Level Monitoring and National Level Monitoring etc. Release 
position during current year is being re viewed regularly with the State/UT 
governments in order to ensure timely releases and effective utilization of 
funds.

People to be benefited under NREG Scheme 
†* 112. SHRI LALIT KISHORE CHATURVEDI: Will the Minister of 
RURAL DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a)whether Government of India have started the implementation of 
National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme and if so, the number of 
targeted people who would be benefited every year and the amount required 
for the same; 
(b)whether creation of permanent assets  and basic infrastructure works is 
possible keeping the proportion of wages and cost of materials; and 
(c) the details regarding the system of implementing, monitoring and 
controlling the said programme? 
THE MINISTER OF RURAL DE VELOPMENT (SHRI RAGHUVANSH 
PRASAD SINGH): (a) The National Rural Employment Guarantee Act 
(NREGA), 2005 has been notified in the Gazette of India on 7th September, 
2005. The notification for applicability of the Act is yet to be issued under 
Section 1 (3) of the Act. About 1.7 crore households are likely to be benefited  
in the first phase of implementation of the scheme and the funds required ' are 
estimated to be of the order of Rs. 17,103 crore for 200 districts. About 4.96 
crore households are likely to be benefited with an estimated expenditure of 
about Rs. 49,600 crore per year when the scheme is extended to cover the 
remaining districts within a period of five years. 
(b)Yes, Sir. Creation of durable assets and strengthening the livelihood 
resource base of the rural poor shall be an important objective of the Scheme 
made under the Act. 
(c) The Panchayats at district, inter-mediate and village levels shall be the 
principal authorities for planning and implementation of the Schemes made 
under the Act. The duties of Panchayats at various levels, District 
Programme Coordinator, Programme Officer and Gram Panchayats have 
been defined in Section 13, 14, 15 and 16  of the Act respectively. The Social 
audit of work shall be done by the Gram Sabha as per the provisions of 
Section 17 of the Act..

Hydroelectricity is a cl ean and renewable source of energy. According to 
the National Electricity Policy, maximum emphasis would be laid on the full 
development of the feasible hydro poten tial in the country. Even with full 
development of the feasible hydro potential in the country, coal would 
necessarily continue to remain the prim ary fuel for meeting future electricity 
demand. 
As per the Policy, for thermal power, economics of generation and supply 
of electricity would be the basis for choice of fuel from among the options 
available. Imported coal based thermal pow er stations, particularly at coastal 
locations, would be encouraged based on their economic viability. 
Use of gas as a fuel for power generation would depend upon its 
availability at reasonable prices. Power sector consumes about 40% of the 
total gas produced in the country. New power generation capacity could 
come up based on indigenous gas findings, which can emerge as a major 
source of power generation if prices  are reasonable. Imported LNG based 
power plants are also a potential source of electricity and the pace of their 
development would depend on their commercial viability. 
Nuclear power is an established sour ce of energy to meet base load 
demand, which contributed about 3% of the electricity generated in 2004-05. 
The current nuclear power capacity in  the country is 3310 MW. Eight 
nuclear power reactors with a total capacity of 3970 MW ace presently under 
construction and on completion of these reactors progressively the nuclear 
power capacity in the country will increase to 7280 MW by end of XI plan. 
The work on these projects is progressing as per schedule. 
The Government has recently accorded in principle approval for setting of 
nuclear power stations of 6800 MW at four sites. These are Kudankulam in 
Tamil Nadu, Jaitapur in Maharashtra, Kakrapar in Gujarat and Rawatbhata in 
Rajasthan. The reactors at Rawatbhata and Kakrapar are based on indigenous 
Pressurized Heavy Water Reactor desi gn. The reactors at Kudankulam and 
Jaitapur are based on reactors to be set up in cooperation with foreign 
countries. Preliminary wo rk in connection with detailed site evaluation is 
being taken up at these sites. This  will be followed up with more power 
reactors so as to reach a capacity of 20000 MW by the year 2020. 
The recent understanding reached with  USA for cooperation in civilian 
nuclear power programme opens up the possibilities of setting up of 
additional nuclear power reactors based on foreign cooperation. The

domestic uranium can support a capacity of 10,000 MW out of which about 
half has already been tied up. Therefor e any private sector participation in 
nuclear power can only be on the basis of external additionality, consistent 
with national and international framework. 
The Electricity Act, 2003 creates a liberal framework for development of 
the electricity industry, promoting competition therein, protecting interest of 
consumers and supply of el ectricity to all areas, rationalization of electricity 
tariff, ensuring transparent policies regarding subsidies, constitution of 
Regulatory Commission and establishmen t of Appellate Tribunal. The Act 
reduces entry barriers in different se gments of power supply industry and 
promotes competition and in turn efficiency improvements. 
Generation has been deficensed by the Act. Transmission, distribution and 
trading are licensed activities and the lic ense is granted by the appropriate 
Electricity Regulatory Commission. Th e Electricity Act, 2003 does not 
discriminate between Private and Public Sector in any of these areas. The Act 
provides for non-discriminatory open  access in transmission from the very 
outset. Open access in distribution is to be introduced by the SERCs in 
phases. 
Section 63 of the Electricity Act, 2003 provides that the Appropriate 
Commission shall adopt the tariff if such tariff has been determined through 
transparent process of bidding in accor dance with the guidelines issued by 
the Central Government Central Government has issued the guidelines for 
competitive bidding for determinaion of tariff for procurement of power by 
distribution licensees. It is expected to facilitate private sector participation in 
generaion. 
The Act also provides for multiple distribution licenses in same area 
through their own distribution system. Central Government has already 
notified the additional requirements for this purpose as stipulated in the Act. 
Under the Electricity Act, 2003 captive power plants, including group 
captive, have been freely permitted. 
Ministry of Power is facilitating financial closure of generation projects. 
An Inter-Institutional Group (IIG) comprising senior representatives from the 
Financial Institutions and Ministry of Power has been constituted to focus on 
fast track power projects which coul d achieve early financial closure.

Alleviation and Rural Development in the country. The Swarnjayanti Gram 
Swarozgar Yojana (SGSY) provides for self employment and the Indira 
Awaas Yojana (IAY) provides shelter to the shelterless rural poor families. 
These schemes are being implemented especially for BPL families living in

Gram Sadak Yojana (PMGSY) for ru ral connectivity, Accelerated Rural 
Water Supply Programme (ARWSP)/Swajaldhara and Central Rural 
Sanitation Programme (CRSP)/Total Sanitation Campaign (TSC) aim at 
development of rural infrastructure and rural amenities. Under TSC, 
however, financial incentive is available only to the BPL households. 
Integrated Wastelands Development Programme (IWDP), Drought Prone 
Area Programme (DPAP) and Desert Development Programme (DDP) are 
area development programmes which are implemented on watershed basis. 
2. The Sampoorna Gramin Rozgar Yojana (SGRY) is a wage empoyment 
programme which is open to all rural poor who are in need of wage 
employment and desire to do manual and unskilled work in and

generated and food-security could be provided through creation of need 
based economic, social and community assets in these Districts. The NFFWP

employment in every financial year to every household whose adult members 
volunteer to do unskilled manual work.

(SHRI SHRIPRAKASH JAISWAL): (a) and (b) "Police" is a State subject as 
per the Constitution of India. As such, it is primarily the responsibility of the 
State Governments of make it transp arent, effective as well as people 
friendly. Government of India has been pursuing with the States to bring 
about the needed reforms in the Police functioning. Modernization of Police 
Forces Schemes is one of the means by which Central Government provides 
assistance to the States. Ministry of  Home Affairs has recently set up an 
Expert Committee to draft a new Po lice Act which should aim at making

registered and printed on Computers. The said scheme is aimed at

827. SHRI DARA SINGH: Will the Minister of DEFENCE be pleased to

philosophy and are guided by operational considerations for ensuring 
territorial integrity. Laying of mines and- demining is carried out in

accordance with well laid down proc edures. It was observed during 
'Operation Parakaram' that some incidents of fatal and non fatal casualties 
occurred resulting in loss of life or disa bility due to mine related accidents in

straying into the minefields by human beings or cattle, sinking or drifting 
away of mines due to the nature of ground and terrain as well as 
environmental conditions or tugging of mines by rodents leading to their

-For person suffering 50—100% disability -Rs. 1.5 Lacs

Potential of wind power energy 
840. SHRI T.T.V. DHINAKARAN: Will the Minister of NON-
CONVENTIONAL ENERGY SOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) the total/estimated potential of wind power energy in the country; 
(b) the total exploitable potential of wind power estimated so far; 
(c) the installed capacity of wind power in the country; and 
(d) the steps taken to exploit more potential of wind power? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF NON-
CONVENTIONAL ENERGY SOURCES (SHRI VILAS MUTTEMWAR): 
(a) The gross wind power potential in the country has been estimated at over 
45,000 M W. Major part of the potential, however, lies in low wind regimes 
having wind power density of 200—300 Watt per square metre. 
(b) The exploitable potential, which is limited by availability of grid 
capacity, is presently about 15,000 MW. 
(c) A total wind power capacity of 4227MW has been installed in the 
country so far. 
(d) Grid interactive wind power proj ects are set up commercially with 
private sector investment. The steps taken by the Government to promote 
setting up of wind power projects include concessional import duty for wind 
electricity generator sub-systems, ex cise duty exemption, ten years tax 
holiday on power projects, benefit of accelerated depreciation and loan from 
Indian Renewable Energy Development Agency (IREDA) and other financial 
institutions. Wind resource assessment studies are supported in various states 
for identifying new areas for deployment of wind power projects. Resource 
assessment, Testing & Certification an d R&D support are being provided by 
the Centre for Wind Energy Technolo gy (C-WET), Chennai, which is an 
autonomous institution under the administrative control of this Ministry.

of solar energy in solving the energy needs of the country in the long run;

to be taken thereon;

entirely without any wastage; and

CONVENTIONAL ENERGY SOURCES (SHRI VILAS MUTTEMWAR): 
(a) and (b) Efforts to assess availability of solar radiation in various parts of 
the country were initiated during early  eighties. In this regard, India 
Meteorological Department (IMD) brought out two handbooks in 1980 and 
1982. The annual average solar energy falling on one square meter of area is 
in the range of 4—7 kilowatt-hour. Pr esently, the Ministry has taken up a 
project with IMD, for updation of the solar radiation data. The project is 
under progress. 
(c) and (d) The Ministry has been promoting development and utilization 
of solar energy in the country. It may be mentioned that every solar system/ 
device has certain losses of incident energy, and only a part of it can be

These include solar water heaters, sola r cookers, solar lanterns, solar home

battery charging applications, etc. Th e focus of research is on further

8. TAX INCENTIVES ON LIQUEFIED NATURAL GAS & NAPHTHA 
(i) CUSTOM DUTY ON IMPORT OF LNG/NAPHTHA 
PRESENT PROVISION 
As per SI. No. 77 of Custom Notification No. 21/2002, import of 
Liquefied Natural Gas/Naphtha is exempted from payment of so much of 
custom duty as in excess of 5%. 
MODIFICATION PROPOSED 
The import of LNG/Naphtha under the above SI. No. may be exempted 
from the payment of custom duty. 
REASON 
Fuel cost of generation (FCOG) based on LNG/Naphtha is needed to be at 
par with FCOG based on other competitive fuel like coal to promote Gas 
based power projects in order to have the following advantages: 
a) It is one of the most clean and green fuel for power generation. 
b) It will provide healthy mixed growth of power sector enhancing fuel 
security. 
c) Power projects based on this fuel are among one of the most efficient. 
As per the India Hydrocarbon Vision  2025, against the present domestic 
gas supply of around 70 MMSCMD, India's demand for Natural Gas by 
2011-12 is projected to be 313 MMSCMD which is unlikely to be met by 
indigenous sources. It will compel sourcing LNG from abroad. 
LIKELY IMPACT 
Since it is a commodity which is imported and the use of these costly fuel 
is limited now, there would not be any significant loss of revenue. 
154 

[30 November, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
On the other hand, the fuel cost of generation is likely to be cheaper by 4%, 
which would be of the order of 8—10 paisa per kwh giving boost to 
economic activities. 
International price of this commodity varies widely from region to region. 
No benchmarked price exists in international market. The price is generally 
negotiated between the contracting parties.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI SURYAKANTA PATIL): (a) No, Sir. 
However, the Ministry had constituted an Expert Group, in 2000, oh the 
Prevention of Alienation of Tribal Land and its Restoration as part of the 
Land Reforms Programme. The Lal Bahadur Shastri National Academy of 
Administration, Mussoorie has conducted State specific assessment studies in 
respect of different States on land reform s. But, these studi es are not at the 
national level for the implementation of land reforms in the States. 
(b) A statement showing the major R ecommendations of the Expert 
Group in brief is annexed. (See below) 
(c) and (d) Land and its management falls within the administrative 
jurisdiction of the respective States as provided under entry No.. 18 of State 
List (List II) of Seventh Schedule to the Constitution of India. The role of the 
Central Government in the field of land reforms is only advisory and 
coordinating. The implementation of Land Reforms programmes are 
reviewed from time to time at various for a including Conferences of 
Revenue Ministers/Secretaries organized by this Ministry. 
In view of these concerted efforts,  the State Governments have so far 
provided ownership rights to 124.22 lakh tenants covering an area of 156.30 
lakh acres. 53.18 lakh beneficiaries have been provided with 49.19 lakh acres 
of ceiling surplus land. 147.47 lakh acres of Government wastelands and 
21.75 acres of Bhoodan land have been distributed to the landless rural poor. 
4.31 lakh acres of alienated tribal land have been restored to the tribal 
community. 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
173 

RAJYA SABHA [30 November, 2005] 
Statement 
Major recommendations of the Expert Group Constituted for land 
reforms 
• Highest priority should be accorded to the preparation and updating 
of land records in tribal areas w ith active participation of tribal 
communities. 
• The land rights of the scheduled tribes extend to land owned by them, 
community lands, forests and water. For recognizing the urgent need 
for survey to record the rights of  tribals, an immediate enjoyment 
survey to establish the rights of the tribal people with a certain 
stipulations is recommended. 
• A campaign mode should be followed for verification of title and 
possession of land. 
• The revenue machinery should enable collection of all documents 
including from the non-government sources facilitating free 
availability for inspection. 
• A village level committee should be constituted for each village in the 
scheduled area for issuing a joint statement indicating the final 
outcome of the survey. 
• Modern technologies should be put to use and computerization of all 
records including digitization of maps and inbuilt updating procedures 
should be resorted to. 
• The community land of the tribals must of recorded in the name of the 
community. 
• The legal provisions prohibiting the alienation of tribal lands in 
Scheduled V Areas and its restoration should be extended to the non-
scheduled areas also. 
• A complete ban on all forms of transfers of tribal lands should be 
enforced. 
• The State Government should think of establishing a Land Bank 
which purchase tribal and non-tribal land being sold and settle the 
same with tribals. 
• Transactions in land should be banned from non-tribals to non-tribals 
in the Scheduled Areas but permitted from non-tribals to tribals. 
174 

[30 November, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
• The law/regulation banning the transf er and alienation of tribal land 
shall prevail over any other law, circular or instruction in force. 
• The process of restoration of the alienated should not be barred by 
any limitation. 
• Jurisdiction for proceedings involvin g transfer or alienation of land 
belonging to Scheduled Tribes shall be exclusively vested with 
prescribed Revenue and Special Courts and civil courts shall have 
jurisdiction in these proceedings. 
• There would be time-bound disposal for completion of these cases 
within a maximum period of three months and the cases shall deemed 
to have been disposed in favour of the tribal litigant, unless it 
disposed by the concerned Court within the time-frame to be fixed. 
• There is an urgent need for rest ricting the number of appeals and 
revisions in the land alienation cases. If the order of the Revenue and 
Special Court is in favour of the tribal, an appeal shall be permitted 
only after execution of the order of such Court by way of physical 
restoration of the disputed land. 
• The District Authorities should be empowered to take suo moto 
action for detection and restoration of land belonging to a member of 
the Scheduled Tribe. 
• In proceedings involvin g transfer of land belonging to Scheduled 
Tribes, oral evidence adduced by a member of the Scheduled tribe 
and the evidence obtained in field enquiry, should be deemed as 
conclusive proof to establish the right and title of the tribal people. In 
all cases involving transfer of land belonging to Scheduled tribes to a 
non-tribal person, the onus of proof that interest in land has been 
legally acquired in accordance with  the provisions of law will be 
squarely on the non-scheduled tribe claimant. 
• All laws should expressly provide that the land shall invariably be 
restored to the tribal people. 
• Where a competent authority has passed an order of restoration of 
land to a Scheduled Tribe claimant, if an appeal or revision petition 
has been filed against this order, the disputed land unless already 
restored to the Scheduled Tribe cl aimant shall be placed in the 
possession of the Government. 
175 

RAJYA SABHA [30 November, 2005] 
• There is an urgent need to inco rporate deterrent measures against 
alienation of land belonging to Scheduled Tribes. 
• A Central guidance be issued to th e State Governments concerned so 
that the Provisions of the Panchayats (Extension to the Scheduled 
Areas) Act, 1996 is effectively implemented. 
• The Expert Group has urged the enactment by Parliament of an 
enabling legislation regarding alienation of land belonging to 
Scheduled Tribes making incorporation of the provisions of the 
enabling legislation as mandatory in all laws/regulations made by the 
respective State Governments in this regard.

(a) what are the criteria on the basis of which BPL census is conducted; 
(b) whether the Government consider the criteria to be foolproof; and 
(c) if not, what steps have been taken to revise the existing criteria of 
identifying the BPL population? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI SURYAKANTA PATIL): (a) to (c) The 
Ministry of Rural Development provides  assistance to the States and Union 
Territories to conduct the BPL Census af ter every five years coinciding with 
the Five Year Plan. The first BPL Cens us was conducted for the 8th Plan in 
1992 and for the 9th Five Year Plan , the BPL Census 1997 was conducted. 
The BPL Census 1992 and BPL Census 1997 which were based on Income 
and Expenditure approach respectively be came subject to criticism because of 
the exclusion criteria. For BPL Census 2002, the Ministry set up an Expert 
Group comprising of Senior Bureaucrats, Academicians, Experts and States 
representatives. After detailed deliberations, the Expert Group recommended a 
'Score Based Ranking' of each household indicating their quality of life for the 
BPL Census 2002. For this purpose, 13 socio-economic indicators including 
size of land holding, type of house, availability of clothes, food security, 
sanitation, literacy, means of livelihood and indebtedness etc. have been 
prescribed. The present methodology to identify BPL families has been 
considered to be an improvement over the previous methodologies as the 
information collected on various parameters can be physically verified.

882. SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA: 
SHRI HARISH RAWAT: 
Will the Minister of TEXTILES be pleased to state: 
(a) it has been more than six months since the phasing out of quota system, 
has Government conducted impact assessment on the rural textile industry of 
the quota phase out and supportive Governments policy initiatives that were 
initiated to support and promote the rural textile industry; 
(b) if so, how the report of the assessment can be accessed; 
(c) what steps have been taken to ensure the livelihood of the rural

quota phase out has been made so far by the Government. Moreover, only

analysis of exports over a period of 1-2 years would be a reasonable period 
for a fair assessment of the impact. 
Export trends after the removal of quota restrictions from 01.01.2005 
indicate that India textile exports to the major markets have shown a 
substantial increase. European Unio n (EU) and the United States (US)

Share of Indian textile industry in international market 
886. SHRI SANJAY RAUT: Will the Minister of TEXTILES be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether Government have taken any new initiatives for expanding 
share of Indian textile industry in international markets; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) what are the main reasons and obstacles for enhancing textile exports 
in the country; and 
(d) how Government are going to tackle these problems for the benefit of 
textile industry? 
THE MINISTER OF TEXTILES (SHRI SHANKERSINH VAGHELA): 
(a) and (b) The Government has been taking a number of steps from time to 
time for the benefit of the Indian textile industry including increasing share 
in international markets. Some of the important initiatives taken are given as 
under:— 
i) 100% Foreign Direct Investment is allowed in the textile sector 
under the automatic route. 
ii) The Government has de-reserve d the readymade garments, hosiery 
and knitwear from the SSI sector. 
iii) The Technology Upgradation Fund Scheme (TUFS) has been made 
operational from 1-4-1999 to facilitate the modernisation and 
upgradation of the sector. 
185 

RAJYA SABHA [30 November, 2005] 
iv) To improve the productivity and quality of cotton, Government has 
launched the Technology Mission on Cotton (TMC). Incentives are 
provided for better farm practices, quality seeds, improvement in 
market infrastructure and modernisation of ginning & pressing 
sector. 
v) To provide the industry with world class infrastructure facilities for 
setting up their textile units, a new scheme namely, 'Scheme for 
Integrated Textile Parks' has been launched by merging existing two 
schemes i.e. Textile Centre Infrastructure Development Scheme 
(TCIDS) and Apparel Park for Exports Scheme (APES). 
Government of India support under the scheme by way of grant or 
equity shall be limited to 40% of the project cost subject to a ceiling 
of Rs. 40 crores. 
vi) 'Apparel Park for Exports Scheme (APES)' was launched with the 
objective of imparting a focused thrust for setting up apparel units of 
international standards at potential growth centres, and to give a 
fillip to exports. Under APES, 12 projects have been sanctioned 
with an estimated support from Government of India of Rs. 191.70 
crores. 
vii) For upgrading infrastructure facilities at important textile centres, 
the 'Textile Centre Infrastructure Development Scheme (TCIDS)' 
was launched. Under TCIDS, 18 projects have been sanctioned with 
an estimated support from Government of India of Rs. 270.80 
crores. 
viii) The fiscal duty structure has been generally rationalised to achieve 
growth and maximum value addition within the country. Except for 
mandatory excise duty on man-made filament yarns and man-made 
staple fibres, the whole value addition chain has been given an 
option of excise expemption. 
ix) The import of specified textiles and garment machinery items has 
been allowed at a concessional ra te of customs duty to encourage 
investments and to make our textile products competitive in the 
global market. The cost of machinery has also been reduced through 
fiscal policy measures. 
x) For the speedy modernisation of the textile processing sector, 
Government has introduced, w.e.f. 20.4.2005, a credit linked capital 
subsidy scheme @ 10% under TUFS, in addition to the existing 5% 
interest reimbursement. 
186 

[30 November, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
xi) The National Institute for Fashion Technology (NIFT), its seven 
branches, and the Apparel Training & Design Centres (ATDCs) are 
running various courses/programmes to meet the skilled manpower 
requirements of the textile industry, especially apparel, in the field 
of design, merchandising and marketing. 
xii) Facilities like eco-testing laborator ies have been created to enable 
exporters to get garments/textiles pre-tested so that they conform to 
the requirements of the importing countries. 
(c) Main obstacles for enhancing textile exports, inter alia, include the 
following:— 
• United States (US), European Union (EU) and Canada account for 
major share of world trade in textiles, and due to the quota 
restrictions imposed by these countries till 31st December, 2004 
under the erstwhile Multi-Fibre Arrangement, India's export growth 
to these markets was restrained. 
• Lack of investments towards modernisation and technological up-
gradation, particularly in weaving and processing segments, are the 
weak areas that have been inhibiting the growth of textile exports in 
real terms. 
• Duty free access to some of our competitors in major markets 
through Preferential Trading Agreement and Generalised Scheme of 
Preferences. 
• High tariff on finished products imposed by some major importing 
countries. 
(d) The steps taken by the Government to tackle the problems have 
been enumerated above in reply to part s (a) & (b) of the question. Further, 
after removal of the quota restrictions, Indian textiles exports to US, EU 
etc. have shown increasing trend.

New handloom policy 
888. SHRI UDAY PRATAP SINGH: 
SHRI V. NARAYANASAMY: 
Will the Minister of TEXTILES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that government have decided to announce new 
handloom policy to ameliorate the sufferings of the weaving community; 
(b) if so, whether it will be announced during the ensuing Winter Session 
of the Parliament; and 
(c) what are main features of the new handloom poilcy? 
THE MINISTER OF TEXTILES (S HRI SHANKERSINH VAGHELA): 
(a) to (c) National Textile Policy was announced in the year 2000. The 
handloom sector also forms a part of the National Textile Policy 2000. The 
details of the National Handloom Policy incorporated in the National Textile 
Policy 2000 are as under:— 
The handloom sector is known for its heritage and the tradition of 
excellent craftsmanship. It provides livelihood to millions of weavers and 
craftsperson. The industry has not only survivedbut also grown over the 
decades due to its inherent strength like flexibility of production in small 
quantities, openness to innovation, low level of capital investment and 
immense possibility of designing fabrics. Government will continue to accord 
priority to this sector. Steps would be taken to promote and develop its 
exclusiveness for the global market. Measure will include the following:— 
• Training modules wilI be developed for weavers engaged in the 
production of low value added items, who may not be able to 
survive the competition consequent on globalization, with the 
objective of upgrading their skills to enable them to find alternate 
employment in the textile or other allied sector; 
188 

[30 November, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
• Comprehensive welfare measures will continue to be implemented 
in close cooperation with the State Governments, for better working 
environment and the social security of the weavers; 
• Effective support systems in research and development, design 
inputs, skill upgradation and market linkages will be provided; 
• The implementation of the Hank Yarn Obligation Order and the 
Reservation Orders issued under the Handloom (Reservation of 
Articles for Production) Act, 1985 will be reviewed keeping in mind 
the needs of the handloom weavers; 
• Weavers Service Centres will be revamped in consonance with the 
contemporary trends, and using Information Technology for 
efficacy, their activities suitably dovetailed with activities of centres 
of design excellence like NIFT and NID; 
• As merchandising and marketing w ill be central to the success of 
the handloom sector, the present package of schemes for production 
of value added fabrics will be streamlined; innovative market-
oriented schemes will be introduced ; and joint ventures encouraged 
both at the domestic and international levels. Brand equity of 
handlooms will be commercially exploited to the extent possible.
